clue.text: Significance of short interval

definitions.meaning: importance or weight, as in a matter of great consequence

explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet speaks of 'enterprises of great pitch and moment' in the same soliloquy the puzzle quotes.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are standard: weight or importance, and a brief instant of time.

clue.text: Like some waves in turbulent sound I sail

indicators.note: turbulent water is churned up, so these letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A sailor notes the choppy water as they set sail across a strait.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turbulent' rearranges SOUNDISAIL; 'sound' looks like noise but is a stretch of sea.
explanation.definitionFit: Sine waves are the textbook smooth oscillation, so sinusoidal describes their shape.

clue.text: Cricket side and coach not in action

parts.note: the off side is one half of a cricket field, the side the batsman faces
a stagecoach, shortened to stage, is an old horse-drawn coach

explanation.surface: A cricket team and its coach sit idle between matches.
explanation.walkthrough: In cricket the field is split into the off side and leg side; a stage was a horse-drawn coach running in stages.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor offstage is out of the scene, so not taking part in the action.

clue.text: In honour of love, repeatedly exquisite

indicators.note: said again, so the pair of pieces is written out twice

parts.note: a toast is drunk to someone, so 'to' means in honour of
love is nil in tennis, the shape of a zero

explanation.surface: A toast is raised to romance, over and over, with gushing praise.
explanation.walkthrough: Hamlet wishes 'this too too solid flesh would melt'; the phrase means affectedly refined.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is an idiom for excessively refined or precious, an over-delicate kind of fineness.

clue.text: Prohibiting in West End a form of audience disapproval

indicators.note: the end of the word West is its final letter

parts.note: an unhappy theatre crowd jeers with boos

explanation.surface: A London theatre bans the crowd from jeering at its shows.
explanation.walkthrough: 'West End' looks like London's theatre district, but 'End' picks the last letter of 'West'.
explanation.definitionFit: To put something under a taboo is to forbid it, so the verb form means banning.

clue.text: Gives inept performance done with woeful cast

parts.note: something done is finished, all over

indicators.note: woefully bad, so the word cast is mangled into another order

explanation.surface: A dreadful troupe of actors botches the show and it's finished.
explanation.walkthrough: 'woeful' signals the rearrangement of the second piece; 'done' means finished, not performed.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamming up a role is exaggerated, unconvincing acting, a poor kind of performance.

clue.text: Player's poor performance is filmed, oddly

indicators.note: behaving oddly, the letters are put into a strange new order

explanation.surface: A sportsperson's bad day is caught on camera in a strange way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'oddly' rearranges ISFILMED; 'oddly' might suggest alternate letters, but those give nothing useful.
explanation.definitionFit: A fielder who fumbles the ball in cricket or baseball has made an error in the field.

clue.text: Player's departure from English team before start of tour

parts.note: XI is eleven, the size of a cricket or football side

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter

explanation.surface: An English side sets off on an overseas tour.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests sport, but the player is an actor leaving the stage, as in the stage direction.
explanation.definitionFit: A stage direction marks an actor's leaving the stage, a departure from the scene.

clue.text: Hamlet, for example, wavering and ultimately indecisive

indicators.note: unsteady, so the word and is shaken into another order
ultimately means at the very end, so the final letter is taken

explanation.surface: The prince famously dithers and never makes up his mind.
explanation.walkthrough: 'wavering' turns AND into DAN; 'ultimately' adds the E ending 'indecisive'. The surface fits Hamlet's famous dithering.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet is the Prince of Denmark, so he is an example of a man from Denmark.

clue.text: Complained as payment's taken back in retirement

indicators.note: one piece is placed inside the other

parts.note: retiring for the night means going to bed

indicators.note: taken back means the word is read in the opposite direction

parts.note: a fee is a payment; the 's stands for 'is'

explanation.surface: A pensioner grumbles because a payment is reclaimed after they stop work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'taken back' turns FEE into EEF, which goes 'in' BED; 'retirement' is going to bed, not leaving work.
explanation.definitionFit: To beef is informal slang for grumbling or making a complaint.

clue.text: For 18 this issue starts on left here

definitions.text: For 18 this issue starts on left here

parts.words: For 18 this issue starts on left here
parts.note: the soliloquist's famous line ends 'that is the' and then this word for an issue; this entry also begins at the grid's left edge

explanation.surface: An editor notes where a speaker's topic begins on the page.
explanation.walkthrough: 18 is SOLILOQUIST: Hamlet's 'To be, or not to be, that is the ...' supplies the word, a synonym of issue, and 10 across starts in the leftmost column.
explanation.definitionFit: An issue under debate is a matter in dispute, a point to be resolved.

clue.text: Able orator adapted a practice of religious work

indicators.note: adapted means altered, so these letters are put into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: A skilled preacher adjusts their approach to church work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'adapted' rearranges ABLEORATOR into ORAETLABOR, and 'a' completes it. The Latin means 'pray and work', the Benedictine motto.
explanation.definitionFit: The Latin motto of Benedictine monks combines prayer and labour as their rule of daily life.

clue.text: Pardon thus in purifying act

indicators.note: the first piece is placed inside the second

parts.note: an ablution is a ritual washing or cleansing
so means thus, in this way

explanation.surface: A ritual cleansing is how forgiveness is granted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' puts the short word inside the ritual-washing word, just after its first two letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A priest grants forgiveness of sins through this formal release from guilt.

clue.text: European learning about evil in this scene of tragedy

indicators.note: one piece wraps around the other

parts.note: lore is traditional knowledge or learning
sin is wrongdoing, evil

explanation.surface: A European scholar reflects on wickedness in a tragic setting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' wraps the learning word round the evil word; 'in' is a link to the definition, the setting of Hamlet.
explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet is set in the Danish castle at Helsingør, the play's location.

clue.text: Troubles around queen, Claudius and Hamlet, say

indicators.note: the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: to trouble someone is to bother them
R is short for regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: Royal intrigues swirl about the queen and the men of the Danish court.
explanation.walkthrough: BOTHERS goes 'around' R. The Hamlet here is the dead king, the prince's father, whose sibling Claudius murdered him.
explanation.definitionFit: Claudius and the elder King Hamlet were siblings, so they are an example of male siblings.

clue.text: Revised section for reviews

indicators.note: revised means altered, so the letters are reworked into a new order

explanation.surface: A rewritten part of the newspaper carries the critics' verdicts.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Revised' rearranges SECTION.
explanation.definitionFit: Critics write reviews of plays, and these are also called notices in the press.

clue.text: Press goes after theatrical group very hard

indicators.note: the second piece follows the first in the answer

parts.note: the cast is the company of actors in a play
to press clothes is to iron them

explanation.surface: Reporters chase after a troupe of actors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Press' looks like journalists but is the verb to iron.
explanation.definitionFit: Cast iron is rigid and brittle, so the term is used figuratively for firm or unbreakable.

clue.text: Eg Laertes, in final act, less sensitive about point

indicators.note: the first piece wraps around the second

parts.note: duller means less sharp or perceptive
E, east, is a point of the compass

explanation.surface: In the last act, Laertes grows callous over a fatal sword point.
explanation.walkthrough: DULLER goes 'about' E. 'point' suggests the poisoned rapier's tip, but it is a compass point.
explanation.definitionFit: Laertes fights Hamlet with rapiers in the last act, making him a swordsman in a formal fight.

clue.text: A single player left in dishonour, quit so disgracefully

indicators.note: the second piece is placed inside the first

parts.note: to soil a name is to dishonour it

indicators.note: behaving disgracefully, the letters fall out of order

explanation.surface: A lone actor walks off in shame, leaving the stage in disgrace.
explanation.walkthrough: L goes 'in' SOIL to make SOLIL; 'disgracefully' rearranges QUITSO into OQUIST.
explanation.definitionFit: An actor delivering a speech alone on stage is one who speaks soliloquies.

clue.text: Estimates — they include 1, 4 across, 10, 21 and 23 for 18

definitions.meaning: a builder's price estimates for a job
famous lines from Hamlet's speeches contain the words at those entries

explanation.walkthrough: 18 is SOLILOQUIST, Hamlet; MOMENT, TOO TOO, QUESTION, ARMS and NO MORE all appear in his soliloquies.
explanation.definitionFit: A tradesman's price offer is a quotation; and lines cited from a play are also quotations.

clue.text: Raised clubs in attempt to wound

indicators.note: in a down entry, raised means read from bottom to top

parts.note: bats are clubs used in cricket or baseball

explanation.surface: Thugs lift their cudgels, intending to injure someone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Raised' turns BATS upward in this down entry.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrust with a knife meant to wound is a jab with a blade.

clue.text: Weapons taken as alternative to taking slings and arrows

definitions.text: taken as alternative to taking slings and arrows
definitions.meaning: Hamlet weighs suffering 'the slings and arrows of outrageous fortune' against taking these against a sea of troubles

explanation.walkthrough: 'slings and arrows' look like weapons, but in the soliloquy they are fortune's blows, to be endured.
explanation.definitionFit: Arms are weapons in general; and Hamlet's alternative to suffering is 'to take arms against a sea of troubles'.

clue.text: Raced inside and verbally attacked

definitions.meaning: rushed into a place at speed

explanation.definitionFit: Literally to rush into somewhere; idiomatically to berate someone harshly.

clue.text: Lacking parts for me? Never again!

definitions.meaning: an out-of-work actor might say there are none of these roles left for them
an exclamation that something will not be repeated

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase also appears in Hamlet's soliloquy: 'To die, to sleep - no more'.
explanation.definitionFit: Both readings work: no further roles available, and a vow that something is finished for good.

clue.text: Present with most suitable ring, having successfully courted

parts.note: the best choice is the most suitable
O is ring-shaped
a suitor who succeeds has won the beloved

explanation.surface: A suitor offers the finest ring after winning their sweetheart's heart.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Present' looks like a gift noun but is the verb, matched by the phrasal verb.
explanation.definitionFit: To present someone with an honour is to confer or grant it on them.

clue.text: Time off for parties in secluded spot

definitions.meaning: a break when Parliament or a court is not sitting, a holiday for the political parties

explanation.walkthrough: 'parties' looks festive but means political parties, whose parliament goes on holiday.
explanation.definitionFit: A parliamentary break is one sense; an alcove or hidden nook is the other.
